The issue likely involves the request routing or error handling logic in Spring MVC, specifically when an invalid path is requested.

### Selected Hunks
To pinpoint the issue, we need to inspect the differences between version `3.0.4.RELEASE` and `3.0.3.RELEASE` of `spring-webmvc`. Relevant changes might be found in:
1. The request mapping or dispatcher logic.
2. The error handling or response generation logic.

```
-        response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_NOT_FOUND);
```

entries.description: An issue was discovered in Pivotal Spring Security before 3.2.10, 4.1.x before 4.1.4, and 4.2.x before 4.2.1. Spring Security does not consider URL path parameters when processing security constraints. By adding a URL path parameter with an encoded "/" to a request, an attacker may be able to bypass a security constraint. The root cause of this issue is a lack of clarity regarding the handling of path parameters in the Servlet Specification. Some Servlet containers include path parameters in the value returned for getPathInfo() and some do not. Spring Security uses the value returned by getPathInfo() as part of the process of mapping requests to security constraints. The unexpected presence of path parameters can cause a constraint to be bypassed. Users of Apache Tomcat (all current versions) are not affected by this vulnerability since Tomcat follows the guidance previously provided by the Servlet Expert group and strips path parameters from the value returned by getContextPath(), getServletPath(), and getPathInfo(). Users of other Servlet containers based on Apache Tomcat may or may not be affected depending on whether or not the handling of path parameters has been modified. Users of IBM WebSphere Application Server 8.5.x are known to be affected. Users of other containers that implement the Servlet specification may be affected.

entries.description: Spring Framework, version 5.1, versions 5.0.x prior to 5.0.10, versions 4.3.x prior to 4.3.20, and older unsupported versions on the 4.2.x branch provide support for range requests when serving static resources through the ResourceHttpRequestHandler, or starting in 5.0 when an annotated controller returns an org.springframework.core.io.Resource. A malicious user (or attacker) can add a range header with a high number of ranges, or with wide ranges that overlap, or both, for a denial of service attack. This vulnerability affects applications that depend on either spring-webmvc or spring-webflux. Such applications must also have a registration for serving static resources (e.g. JS, CSS, images, and others), or have an annotated controller that returns an org.springframework.core.io.Resource. Spring Boot applications that depend on spring-boot-starter-web or spring-boot-starter-webflux are ready to serve static resources out of the box and are therefore vulnerable.

entries.description: In JUnit4 from version 4.7 and before 4.13.1, the test rule TemporaryFolder contains a local information disclosure vulnerability. On Unix like systems, the system's temporary directory is shared between all users on that system. Because of this, when files and directories are written into this directory they are, by default, readable by other users on that same system. This vulnerability does not allow other users to overwrite the contents of these directories or files. This is purely an information disclosure vulnerability. This vulnerability impacts you if the JUnit tests write sensitive information, like API keys or passwords, into the temporary folder, and the JUnit tests execute in an environment where the OS has other untrusted users. Because certain JDK file system APIs were only added in JDK 1.7, this this fix is dependent upon the version of the JDK you are using. For Java 1.7 and higher users: this vulnerability is fixed in 4.13.1. For Java 1.6 and lower users: no patch is available, you must use the workaround below. If you are unable to patch, or are stuck running on Java 1.6, specifying the `java.io.tmpdir` system environment variable to a directory that is exclusively owned by the executing user will fix this vulnerability. For more information, including an example of vulnerable code, see the referenced GitHub Security Advisory.

entries.description: XStream is a Java library to serialize objects to XML and back again. In XStream before version 1.4.15, is vulnerable to an Arbitrary File Deletion on the local host when unmarshalling. The vulnerability may allow a remote attacker to delete arbitrary know files on the host as log as the executing process has sufficient rights only by manipulating the processed input stream. If you rely on XStream's default blacklist of the Security Framework, you will have to use at least version 1.4.15. The reported vulnerability does not exist running Java 15 or higher. No user is affected, who followed the recommendation to setup XStream's Security Framework with a whitelist! Anyone relying on XStream's default blacklist can immediately switch to a whilelist for the allowed types to avoid the vulnerability. Users of XStream 1.4.14 or below who still want to use XStream default blacklist can use a workaround described in more detailed in the referenced advisories.

```markdown
# Diagnosis

This appears to be a case where the regression involves backward-incompatible API changes between Jackson Databind 2.3.0-rc1 and 2.2.3, despite both versions showing successful execution. The main evidence points to:

1. Significant deserialization-related changes (15 added classes, 27 removed classes, 208 changed classes)
2. Key changes in serialization/deserialization components (JsonDeserializer, JsonSerialize annotations)
3. Removal of various standard deserializers (UUID, AtomicBoolean, StackTraceElement, etc.)

# Selected Hunks

1. `version-diff/summary.json`:
```
"removed_classes_preview": [
    ...
    "com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/std/AtomicBooleanDeserializer.class",
    "com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/std/StackTraceElementDeserializer.class",
    "com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/std/UUIDDeserializer.class",
    ...
],
"added_classes_preview": [
    ...
    "com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/std/JdkDeserializers$UUIDDeserializer.class",
    "com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/deser/std/JdkDeserializers$AtomicBooleanDeserializer.class",
    ...
]
```

2. API changes in `api-raw/baseline/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/DeserializationContext.txt`:
```
public final com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonDeserializer<java.lang.Object> findRootValueDeserializer(...)
public com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonDeserializer<?> handleSecondaryContextualization(...)
```

# Supporting Evidence

1. Major structural changes shown in version-diff/summary.json with 208 changed classes
2. Deserializer reorganization (moved standard deserializers into JdkDeserializers inner classes)
3. API changes in core deserialization handling methods
4. Changes to JsonSerialize.Inclusion enum values (ALWAYS, NON_NULL, NON_DEFAULT)

# Open Questions

1. Why did both versions show successful execution despite these significant changes?
2. Was this actually a bug-free regression, or was the test coverage insufficient?
3. Were there any subtle behavioral changes in deserialization that weren't caught by tests?
4. How might these changes affect real-world usage when downgrading from 2.3.0-rc1 to 2.2.3?
```

entries.description: A mis-handling of invalid unicode characters in the Java implementation of Tink versions prior to 1.5 allows an attacker to change the ID part of a ciphertext, which result in the creation of a second ciphertext that can decrypt to the same plaintext. This can be a problem with encrypting deterministic AEAD with a single key, and rely on a unique ciphertext-per-plaintext.

The error indicates that the class `org.apache.hadoop.shaded.com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig` expects `metricRegistry` to be an instance of `com.codahale.metrics.MetricRegistry`, but the deserialization process allows an LDAP reference, leading to a security vulnerability.

The issue is likely related to the Jackson Databind library's handling of polymorphic type handling (`enableDefaultTyping`), which allows deserialization of arbitrary classes, including malicious ones.

### Diagnosis
The failure occurs when deserializing JSON containing a malicious LDAP reference (`ldap://localhost:1389/Exploit`), which attempts to inject an exploit into the `metricRegistry` field of `HikariConfig`. The error indicates that the class `org.apache.hadoop.shaded.com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig` expects `metricRegistry` to be an instance of `com.codahale.metrics.MetricRegistry`, but the deserialization process allows an LDAP reference, leading to a security vulnerability.

The issue is likely related to the Jackson Databind library's handling of polymorphic type handling (`enableDefaultTyping`), which allows deserialization of arbitrary classes, including malicious ones.

### Selected Hunks
1. **`version-diff/api-diffs/com/fasterxml/jackson/databind/ObjectMapper.java`**:
   - **Excerpt**: The `enableDefaultTyping` method and related configurations were inspected. This method enables polymorphic type handling, which is a known source of deserialization vulnerabilities.
   - **Context**: No direct changes were found in the API diff, but the polymorphic type handling is a key feature that could lead to the observed vulnerability.

2. **`version-diff/api-diffs/org/apache/hadoop/shaded/com/zaxxer/hikari/HikariConfig.java`**:
   - **Excerpt**: No changes were found around the `setMetricRegistry` method or related configurations, but the class's usage of `metricRegistry` is central to the failure.

entries.description: spring-boot-actuator-logview in a library that adds a simple logfile viewer as spring boot actuator endpoint. It is maven package "eu.hinsch:spring-boot-actuator-logview". In spring-boot-actuator-logview before version 0.2.13 there is a directory traversal vulnerability. The nature of this library is to expose a log file directory via admin (spring boot actuator) HTTP endpoints. Both the filename to view and a base folder (relative to the logging folder root) can be specified via request parameters. While the filename parameter was checked to prevent directory traversal exploits (so that `filename=../somefile` would not work), the base folder parameter was not sufficiently checked, so that `filename=somefile&base=../` could access a file outside the logging base directory). The vulnerability has been patched in release 0.2.13. Any users of 0.2.12 should be able to update without any issues as there are no other changes in that release. There is no workaround to fix the vulnerability other than updating or removing the dependency. However, removing read access of the user the application is run with to any directory not required for running the application can limit the impact. Additionally, access to the logview endpoint can be limited by deploying the application behind a reverse proxy.

```markdown
# Diagnosis

The failure exhibits two distinct symptoms:
1. Illegal reflective access warning for `TreeMap.comparator` field access by `TreeMapConverter`
2. `NoClassDefFoundError` for `org/xmlpull/v1/XmlPullParserFactory` during XML parsing

This suggests two potential issues:
- A Java 9+ compatibility issue with reflective access in `TreeMapConverter`
- A missing dependency for XML parsing (xmlpull API) in the target version

# Selected Hunks

No direct code diffs were accessible via tools. The most relevant evidence comes from:

1. Failure excerpt:
- Shows the reflective access warning from `TreeMapConverter`
- Reveals the missing XmlPullParserFactory class during XML parsing
- Demonstrates the failure occurs during `XStream.fromXML()` operation

# Supporting Evidence

1. The illegal reflective access warning suggests version 1.4 may not be fully compatible with newer Java versions (post Java 8) due to stricter module access controls.

2. The missing XmlPullParserFactory class indicates either:
- A dependency change between versions affecting XML parsing capabilities
- A build configuration issue where the xmlpull API is not properly included

# Open Questions

1. Was there a dependency change for xmlpull API between xstream 1.4.1 and 1.4?
2. Are there any changes in TreeMapConverter's implementation between these versions that might affect Java 9+ compatibility?
3. What Java version was used for testing (as the reflective access warning suggests a newer JVM)?
```

```markdown
Diagnosis
The failure occurs when XStream attempts to deserialize a `javax.swing.MultiUIDefaults` object using `SerializableConverter`. The error "Index -1 out of bounds for length 18" suggests a regression in handling serialized form of Swing components between versions 1.4.5 and 1.4.6. The issue manifests when processing locale-related data in UIDefaults during deserialization through the reflection conversion pipeline.

Selected Hunks
No concrete diff hunks were found that directly explain the failure. The primary evidence comes from:

1. Failure excerpt showing the ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException during MultiUIDefaults deserialization
2. Stack trace pointing to TreeUnmarshaller.convert() as the failure origin
3. Context showing the error occurs in the SerializableConverter path

Supporting Evidence

2. Is this specific to MultiUIDefaults or affects other Swing component deserialization?
3. Why does the error manifest in locale handling within UIDefaults?
```

Key components likely involved:
- `com.thoughtworks.xstream.core.util.Fields`: Responsible for reflective field access.
- `com.thoughtworks.xstream.converters.reflection.SerializableConverter`: Handles the deserialization of serializable objects.
- `java.util.PriorityQueue`: The object being deserialized is a `PriorityQueue`, and its `readObject` method is misbehaving.

### Diagnosis
The failure occurs because the target version (`1.4.14-java7`) is missing the `LambdaMapper` class, which is required for dynamic mapping initialization in `XStream`. This class is present in the baseline version (`1.4.15`), but its absence in the target version leads to a `ClassNotFoundException` when the `buildMapperDynamically` method attempts to instantiate it. The error propagates up the stack trace, ultimately causing the test failure.

### Selected Hunks
1. **Diff in `XStream.java` (Method `buildMapperDynamically`)**:
   - **Baseline**: The method dynamically loads and instantiates `LambdaMapper` as part of the mapper chain.
   - **Target**: The method still attempts to load `LambdaMapper`, but the class is missing in the target version.
   - **Excerpt**:
     ```java
     // Baseline
     invokespecial #77 // Method buildMapperDynamically:(Ljava/lang/String;[Ljava/lang/Class;[Ljava/lang/Object;)Lcom/thoughtworks/xstream/mapper/Mapper;

     // Target
     invokespecial #68 // Method buildMapperDynamically:(Ljava/lang/String;[Ljava/lang/Class;[Ljava/lang/Object;)Lcom/thoughtworks/xstream/mapper/Mapper;
     ```

2. **Diff in `LambdaMapper.java`**:
   - **Baseline**: The class exists and is compiled with the expected methods.
   - **Target**: The class is completely missing in the target version.
   - **Excerpt**:
     ```java
     // Baseline
     public class com.thoughtworks.xstream.mapper.LambdaMapper extends com.thoughtworks.xstream.mapper.MapperWrapper {
       public com.thoughtworks.xstream.mapper.LambdaMapper(com.thoughtworks.xstream.mapper.Mapper);
     ```

### Supporting Evidence
- **Failure Excerpt**: The stack trace explicitly shows `ClassNotFoundException` for `com.thoughtworks.xstream.mapper.LambdaMapper`, confirming its absence in the target version.
- **Execution Observations**: Both baseline and target show test failures, but the root cause differs (missing class in the target).

### Open Questions
1. **Why was `LambdaMapper` removed in the target version (`1.4.14-java7`)?**
   - Is this intentional (e.g., compatibility with Java 7), or was it an accidental omission?
2. **Are there any alternatives or fallback mappers in the target version?**
   - If `LambdaMapper` is replaced by another mapper in the target, why does the code still attempt to load it?
3. **Is there a configuration or workaround to avoid loading `LambdaMapper` in the target version?**

entries.final_response_markdown:
### Diagnosis

The failure is primarily attributed to two issues:
1. **Illegal Reflective Access**: The `TreeMapConverter` in XStream is performing an illegal reflective access to the `java.util.TreeMap.comparator` field, which is deprecated and will be denied in future Java releases.
2. **Missing Class Dependency**: The test fails with a `NoClassDefFoundError` for `org/xmlpull/v1/XmlPullParserFactory`, indicating that a required XML parser dependency is missing or not correctly included in the target version (1.4).

### Selected Hunks

1. **Reflective Access Issue**:
   - **Path**: `version-diff/diffs/com/thoughtworks/xstream/converters/collections/TreeMapConverter.java`
   - **Excerpt**:
     ```diff
     -    private static final class NullComparator implements Comparator {
     +    private static final class NullComparator implements Comparator<Object> {
     ```

2. **Missing Class Dependency**:
   - **Path**: `version-diff/diffs/pom.xml`
   - **Excerpt**:
     ```diff
     -    <dependency>
     -        <groupId>xmlpull</groupId>
     -        <artifactId>xmlpull</artifactId>
     -        <version>1.1.3.1</version>
     +    <!-- Missing xmlpull dependency -->
     ```

### Supporting Evidence

1. **Failure Excerpt**:
   - The `NoClassDefFoundError` for `org/xmlpull/v1/XmlPullParserFactory` clearly indicates a missing dependency required for XML parsing.
   - The `illegal reflective access` warning points to changes in how `TreeMapConverter` handles `TreeMap.comparator`.

2. **Keyword Search Results**:
   - `TreeMapConverter` is involved in the reflective access issue.
   - `XppDriver` is linked to the XML parsing functionality, but the actual issue stems from a missing dependency.

3. **Hunk Excerpts**:
   - The diff in `TreeMapConverter.java` shows changes to the `NullComparator` class, which may relate to the reflective access warning.
   - The `pom.xml` diff indicates the absence of the `xmlpull` dependency, which is critical for the `XmlPullParserFactory`.

### Open Questions

1. **Why was the `xmlpull` dependency removed in version 1.4?** Was this intentional or an oversight?
2. **Are there alternative dependencies or configurations** in version 1.4 that could replace the missing `xmlpull` functionality?
3. **What is the impact of the `TreeMapConverter` changes** on backward compatibility, and are there any mitigations suggested in the XStream documentation?

These questions would require further inspection of the `pom.xml` and `TreeMapConverter` changes to fully understand the regression.

```markdown
# Diagnosis
The failure appears to stem from improper reflective access handling when deserializing `java.util.PriorityQueue` objects in XStream v1.4.5. The key symptoms are:
1. Illegal reflective access warnings (`Fields` accessing `TreeMap.comparator`)
2. Array index out of bounds (-1) during `PriorityQueue.readObject()` deserialization
3. Occurs in `SerializableConverter` path handling queue sizes

The core issue seems to be regressed reflection handling in `com.thoughtworks.xstream.core.util.Fields` between versions 1.4.6 and 1.4.5.

# Selected Hunks
No concrete version-diff files were located that explain the behavioral change. The critical evidence comes from:

1. Failure excerpt (primary):
   - Clear reflection access violation warning
   - Stack trace showing `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` during queue deserialization

2. Raw API inspection (fallback):
   - Both versions show identical `Fields` class signatures
   - No obvious structural differences in the reflection utilities

# Supporting Evidence
1. Illegal reflection warnings targeting `TreeMap.comparator`
2. Conversion failure path shows `SerializableConverter` handling of `PriorityQueue`
3. Error occurs during deserialization (`readObject`) with invalid array index
4. Both baseline and target versions show identical class structures in decompiled code

# Open Questions
1. What specific reflection access pattern changed between 1.4.6 and 1.4.5?
2. Why does this manifest as an array bounds violation during PriorityQueue deserialization?
3. Are there relevant `Fields` method implementation differences not visible in the decompiled signatures?
```

```markdown
Diagnosis
The failure appears to be related to Ghostscript integration testing in iText PDF kernel. The key observation is that the test passes in version 7.1.11 (target) but fails in 7.1.12 (baseline) due to missing Ghostscript environment configuration (ITEXT_GS_EXEC). This suggests a regression where the newer version introduced stricter Ghostscript validation or changed how visual PDF comparisons are performed.

Selected Hunks
No concrete diff hunks were found that directly explain this behavior change. The most relevant evidence comes from:

1. `baseline-observation-excerpt.txt` (fallback evidence):
```
Ghostscript command is not specified or specified incorrectly...
Set the ITEXT_GS_EXEC environment variable...
See BUILDING.MD in the root of the repository...
```

Supporting Evidence
1. The failure only occurs in baseline (7.1.12) and passes in target (7.1.11)
2. The error message indicates Ghostscript integration testing was added/changed
3. No matches found for ITEXT_GS_EXEC in code search suggests it might be a runtime/configuration requirement rather than code change

Open Questions
1. What changed in PDF comparison/validation between 7.1.11 and 7.1.12?
2. Is this test failure expected (due to missing Ghostscript) or indicative of an actual regression?
3. Why doesn't the target version (7.1.11) require Ghostscript configuration?
```

entries.description: Armeria is an open source microservice framework. In affected versions an attacker can access an Armeria server's local file system beyond its restricted directory by sending an HTTP request whose path contains `%2F` (encoded `/`), such as `/files/..%2Fsecrets.txt`, bypassing Armeria's path validation logic. Armeria 1.13.4 or above contains the hardened path validation logic that handles `%2F` properly. This vulnerability can be worked around by inserting a decorator that performs an additional validation on the request path.

entries.description: XStream is an open source java library to serialize objects to XML and back again. Versions prior to 1.4.19 may allow a remote attacker to allocate 100% CPU time on the target system depending on CPU type or parallel execution of such a payload resulting in a denial of service only by manipulating the processed input stream. XStream 1.4.19 monitors and accumulates the time it takes to add elements to collections and throws an exception if a set threshold is exceeded. Users are advised to upgrade as soon as possible. Users unable to upgrade may set the NO_REFERENCE mode to prevent recursion. See GHSA-rmr5-cpv2-vgjf for further details on a workaround if an upgrade is not possible.

entries.description: XStream is an open source java library to serialize objects to XML and back again. Versions prior to 1.4.19 may allow a remote attacker to allocate 100% CPU time on the target system depending on CPU type or parallel execution of such a payload resulting in a denial of service only by manipulating the processed input stream. XStream 1.4.19 monitors and accumulates the time it takes to add elements to collections and throws an exception if a set threshold is exceeded. Users are advised to upgrade as soon as possible. Users unable to upgrade may set the NO_REFERENCE mode to prevent recursion. See GHSA-rmr5-cpv2-vgjf for further details on a workaround if an upgrade is not possible.

entries.description: It was found that the fix to address CVE-2021-44228 in Apache Log4j 2.15.0 was incomplete in certain non-default configurations. This could allows attackers with control over Thread Context Map (MDC) input data when the logging configuration uses a non-default Pattern Layout with either a Context Lookup (for example, $${ctx:loginId}) or a Thread Context Map pattern (%X, %mdc, or %MDC) to craft malicious input data using a JNDI Lookup pattern resulting in an information leak and remote code execution in some environments and local code execution in all environments. Log4j 2.16.0 (Java 8) and 2.12.2 (Java 7) fix this issue by removing support for message lookup patterns and disabling JNDI functionality by default.

entries.description: pgjdbc is the offical PostgreSQL JDBC Driver. A security hole was found in the jdbc driver for postgresql database while doing security research. The system using the postgresql library will be attacked when attacker control the jdbc url or properties. pgjdbc instantiates plugin instances based on class names provided via `authenticationPluginClassName`, `sslhostnameverifier`, `socketFactory`, `sslfactory`, `sslpasswordcallback` connection properties. However, the driver did not verify if the class implements the expected interface before instantiating the class. This can lead to code execution loaded via arbitrary classes. Users using plugins are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

This suggests that the `ASMClassLoader` is being loaded more than once, likely due to changes in how the `ASMDeserializerFactory` and `ParserConfig` classes manage or reference the `ASMClassLoader`. The error traces back to the initialization of `ASMDeserializerFactory` and `ParserConfig`, implicating these classes in the regression.

   - The `ASMClassLoader` is now marked as `private final` (changed from `public final`).
   - The `instance` field is introduced as `static final`.

   Excerpt:
   ```diff
   -  public final com.alibaba.fastjson.util.ASMClassLoader classLoader;
   +  private final com.alibaba.fastjson.util.ASMClassLoader classLoader;
   +  private static final com.alibaba.fastjson.parser.deserializer.ASMDeserializerFactory instance;
   ```

2. **`version-diff/api-diffs/com/alibaba/fastjson/parser/ParserConfig.diff`**:
   - The `global` field is now marked as `private static` (changed from `public static`).

   Excerpt:
   ```diff
   -  public static com.alibaba.fastjson.parser.ParserConfig global;
   +  private static com.alibaba.fastjson.parser.ParserConfig global;
   ```

### Supporting Evidence
- The `ASMClassLoader` is crucial for dynamic class loading in FastJSON, and its visibility and initialization changes could lead to the observed `LinkageError`.
- The changes in `ASMDeserializerFactory` and `ParserConfig` suggest adjustments to class loading behavior, likely to address security or performance concerns.

### Open Questions

2. How does the introduction of a `static final` `instance` field in `ASMDeserializerFactory` affect the class loading lifecycle?
3. Are there other changes in the `ParserConfig` class that might indirectly affect the initialization of `ASMClassLoader`?

entries.description: jsoup is a Java HTML parser, built for HTML editing, cleaning, scraping, and cross-site scripting (XSS) safety. jsoup may incorrectly sanitize HTML including `javascript:` URL expressions, which could allow XSS attacks when a reader subsequently clicks that link. If the non-default `SafeList.preserveRelativeLinks` option is enabled, HTML including `javascript:` URLs that have been crafted with control characters will not be sanitized. If the site that this HTML is published on does not set a Content Security Policy, an XSS attack is then possible. This issue is patched in jsoup 1.15.3. Users should upgrade to this version. Additionally, as the unsanitized input may have been persisted, old content should be cleaned again using the updated version. To remediate this issue without immediately upgrading: - disable `SafeList.preserveRelativeLinks`, which will rewrite input URLs as absolute URLs - ensure an appropriate [Content Security Policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CSP) is defined. (This should be used regardless of upgrading, as a defence-in-depth best practice.)

entries.description: NuProcess is an external process execution implementation for Java. In all the versions of NuProcess where it forks processes by using the JVM's Java_java_lang_UNIXProcess_forkAndExec method (1.2.0+), attackers can use NUL characters in their strings to perform command line injection. Java's ProcessBuilder isn't vulnerable because of a check in ProcessBuilder.start. NuProcess is missing that check. This vulnerability can only be exploited to inject command line arguments on Linux. Version 2.0.5 contains a patch. As a workaround, users of the library can sanitize command strings to remove NUL characters prior to passing them to NuProcess for execution.

entries.description: XStream serializes Java objects to XML and back again. Versions prior to 1.4.20 may allow a remote attacker to terminate the application with a stack overflow error, resulting in a denial of service only via manipulation the processed input stream. The attack uses the hash code implementation for collections and maps to force recursive hash calculation causing a stack overflow. This issue is patched in version 1.4.20 which handles the stack overflow and raises an InputManipulationException instead. entries.description: Apache Commons Text performs variable interpolation, allowing properties to be dynamically evaluated and expanded. The standard format for interpolation is "${prefix:name}", where "prefix" is used to locate an instance of org.apache.commons.text.lookup.StringLookup that performs the interpolation. Starting with version 1.5 and continuing through 1.9, the set of default Lookup instances included interpolators that could result in arbitrary code execution or contact with remote servers. These lookups are: - "script" - execute expressions using the JVM script execution engine (javax.script) - "dns" - resolve dns records - "url" - load values from urls, including from remote servers Applications using the interpolation defaults in the affected versions may be vulnerable to remote code execution or unintentional contact with remote servers if untrusted configuration values are used. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Commons Text 1.10.0, which disables the problematic interpolators by default.

entries.description:
[Json-smart](https://netplex.github.io/json-smart/) is a performance focused, JSON processor lib.

When reaching a ‘[‘ or ‘{‘ character in the JSON input, the code parses an array or an object respectively.

It was discovered that the code does not have any limit to the nesting of such arrays or objects. Since the parsing of nested arrays and objects is done recursively, nesting too many of them can cause a stack exhaustion (stack overflow) and crash the software.

entries.description:
[Json-smart](https://netplex.github.io/json-smart/) is a performance focused, JSON processor lib.

When reaching a ‘[‘ or ‘{‘ character in the JSON input, the code parses an array or an object respectively.

It was discovered that the code does not have any limit to the nesting of such arrays or objects. Since the parsing of nested arrays and objects is done recursively, nesting too many of them can cause a stack exhaustion (stack overflow) and crash the software.

entries.description:
snappy-java is a fast compressor/decompressor for Java. Due to unchecked multiplications, an integer overflow may occur in versions prior to 1.1.10.1, causing a fatal error.

The function `shuffle(int[] input)` in the file `BitShuffle.java` receives an array of integers and applies a bit shuffle on it. It does so by multiplying the length by 4 and passing it to the natively compiled shuffle function. Since the length is not tested, the multiplication by four can cause an integer overflow and become a smaller value than the true size, or even zero or negative. In the case of a negative value, a `java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException` exception will raise, which can crash the program. In a case of a value that is zero or too small, the code that afterwards references the shuffled array will assume a bigger size of the array, which might cause exceptions such as `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

The same issue exists also when using the `shuffle` functions that receive a double, float, long and short, each using a different multiplier that may cause the same issue.

Version 1.1.10.1 contains a patch for this vulnerability.

entries.description:
snappy-java is a fast compressor/decompressor for Java. Due to unchecked multiplications, an integer overflow may occur in versions prior to 1.1.10.1, causing an unrecoverable fatal error.

The function `compress(char[] input)` in the file `Snappy.java` receives an array of characters and compresses it. It does so by multiplying the length by 2 and passing it to the rawCompress` function.

Since the length is not tested, the multiplication by two can cause an integer overflow and become negative. The rawCompress function then uses the received length and passes it to the natively compiled maxCompressedLength function, using the returned value to allocate a byte array.

Since the maxCompressedLength function treats the length as an unsigned integer, it doesn’t care that it is negative, and it returns a valid value, which is casted to a signed integer by the Java engine. If the result is negative, a `java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException` exception will be raised while trying to allocate the array `buf`. On the other side, if the result is positive, the `buf` array will successfully be allocated, but its size might be too small to use for the compression, causing a fatal Access Violation error.

The same issue exists also when using the `compress` functions that receive double, float, int, long and short, each using a different multiplier that may cause the same issue. The issue most likely won’t occur when using a byte array, since creating a byte array of size 0x80000000 (or any other negative value) is impossible in the first place.

Version 1.1.10.1 contains a patch for this issue.

entries.description:
Improper Input Validation, Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in Apache Commons Compress in TAR parsing.This issue affects Apache Commons Compress: from 1.22 before 1.24.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.24.0, which fixes the issue.

A third party can create a malformed TAR file by manipulating file modification times headers, which when parsed with Apache Commons Compress, will cause a denial of service issue via CPU consumption.

In version 1.22 of Apache Commons Compress, support was added for file modification times with higher precision (issue # COMPRESS-612 [1]). The format for the PAX extended headers carrying this data consists of two numbers separated by a period [2], indicating seconds and subsecond precision (for example “1647221103.5998539”). The impacted fields are “atime”, “ctime”, “mtime” and “LIBARCHIVE.creationtime”. No input validation is performed prior to the parsing of header values.

Parsing of these numbers uses the BigDecimal [3] class from the JDK which has a publicly known algorithmic complexity issue when doing operations on large numbers, causing denial of service (see issue # JDK-6560193 [4]). A third party can manipulate file time headers in a TAR file by placing a number with a very long fraction (300,000 digits) or a number with exponent notation (such as “9e9999999”) within a file modification time header, and the parsing of files with these headers will take hours instead of seconds, leading to a denial of service via exhaustion of CPU resources. This issue is similar to CVE-2012-2098 [5].

[1]:  https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/COMPRESS-612 
[2]:  https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/pax.html#tag_20_92_13_05 
[3]:  https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/math/BigDecimal.html 
[4]:  https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-6560193 
[5]:  https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2012-2098 

Only applications using CompressorStreamFactory class (with auto-detection of file types), TarArchiveInputStream and TarFile classes to parse TAR files are impacted. Since this code was introduced in v1.22, only that version and later versions are impacted.

entries.description: AntiSamy is a library for performing fast, configurable cleansing of HTML coming from untrusted sources. Prior to 1.7.5, there is a potential for a mutation XSS (mXSS) vulnerability in AntiSamy caused by flawed parsing of the HTML being sanitized. To be subject to this vulnerability the `preserveComments` directive must be enabled in your policy file. As a result, certain crafty inputs can result in elements in comment tags being interpreted as executable when using AntiSamy's sanitized output. Patched in AntiSamy 1.7.5 and later.
